meta.title: Who really said "Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Peter Drucker really did draw this distinction — but his 1974 book reads “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right.” The one-liner is a compression.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things'?
meta.ogDescription: Drucker put the efficiency/effectiveness line in print in 1974 — two words longer than the version everyone quotes. The full chronology, 1869 to 1997.

answer.label: Attributed to

answer.sourceLine: Drucker really did draw this contrast in print: Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (Harper & Row, 1974) reads “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.” The tidy semicolon version everyone quotes is that same sentence with “is concerned with” compressed back to “is” — two words shorter — and no Drucker text has been documented carrying the compressed wording verbatim.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually appears

docMeta.dd: “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right” — two words longer than the popular version

source.excerpt: Effectiveness is the foundation of success—efficiency is a minimum condition for survival after success has been achieved. Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.
trail: 1869 and 1934 — the shape of the sentence predates Drucker. Quote Investigator ↗ records an 1869 filler item in the Harrisburg Telegraph — “There is a difference between doing a thing right, and doing the right thing” — and a 1934 Elsie Robinson column arguing that efficiency means knowing what the right thing to do is. Neither uses the word “effectiveness.”

May 1963 — Drucker joins the two words. His article “Managing for Business Effectiveness” ↗ ran in Harvard Business Review; Quote Investigator ↗ quotes it on the confusion between effectiveness and efficiency that stands between doing the right things and doing things right.

1974 — the closest thing to the quotation. Page 45 of Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices carries the sentence pair in full, verified with scans ↗. QI concludes Drucker can reasonably be credited with the efficiency-versus-effectiveness versions of 1963, 1965 and 1974.

The other famous version is Bennis, not Drucker. Barry Popik ↗ traces “Managers do things right; leaders do the right thing” to Warren G. Bennis and Burt Nanus’s Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge (1985), and QI credits Bennis for the leading-versus-managing wording in his 1997 Managing People Is Like Herding Cats.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, whose bibliographic note records the passage as verified with scans of the Harper & Row edition. Note the second sentence matches the popular quotation word for word; only the first was shortened in circulation.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: About Peter Drucker
author.metaLine: 1909–2005 · Austrian-American management consultant, educator and author
author.bio: Peter Ferdinand Drucker was born in Vienna in 1909 and died in Claremont, California, in 2005. He is generally treated as the founder of modern management as a field of study, and his books — among them The Practice of Management, The Effective Executive and the vast 1974 textbook Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices — introduced ideas now so absorbed into business language that they read as common sense. He described himself not as a management theorist but as a social ecologist, interested in how institutions shape the people inside them.

misattribution.heading: What gets muddled
misattribution.intro: Putting Drucker’s name on this is not a mistake — he is the right man. But four separate things travel under his name, and none of them is his exact printed sentence — that is below.

items.why: What Drucker printed in 1974 was “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.” The circulating one-liner deletes “is concerned with” and swaps the full stop for a semicolon. Quote Investigator ↗ titles its investigation with Drucker’s longer wording for exactly this reason.

“Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things” is a different saying with a different owner. Stephen R. Covey put that line in The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989) and credited it to Drucker and Bennis jointly; Quote Investigator ↗ finds the evidence points to Bennis for the leading-versus-managing framing.

items.scope: The book it gets cited to
items.why: The quotation is routinely footnoted to Drucker’s 1967 book. Barry Popik ↗ writes only that Drucker “said something like this in 1960s lectures and in his book, The Effective Executive (1967)” — a hedge, not a page reference. The sources actually documented with text are the 1963 article, the 1965 lecture and the 1974 book.

items.who: an 1869 newspaper filler and columnist Elsie Robinson
items.why: The right-thing/thing-right wordplay was in print long before management theory existed: an 1869 Harrisburg Telegraph item and a 1934 Elsie Robinson column both use it, as Quote Investigator ↗ documents. Drucker’s contribution was attaching it to the pair of business terms.

misattribution.truthLine: Drucker’s own sentence, verified against scans of the 1974 edition ↗, runs two words longer: “Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.”

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: Drucker’s complaint in the May 1963 Harvard Business Review was not philosophical, it was practical: every tool a manager had — above all the accounting numbers — measured how well things were being done, and none of them asked whether those things were worth doing. The efficiency/effectiveness pairing was his way of naming the missing measurement.

The phrasing survives because of its shape. It is an antimetabole — the same words returned in reversed order — which is why it compresses so easily, and why it kept mutating: efficiency versus effectiveness, management versus leadership, CEO versus COO. Each generation of business writers reset the two nouns and kept the frame.
detailsBody: In 1965 The Financial Post of Toronto printed a digest of a Drucker lecture at the University of Toronto in which he set the pair out at length, arguing that a business can die of inefficiency but that no business grows merely because it is efficient. Quote Investigator reproduces the passage.

The shortened phrasing was circulating well before the 1974 book. Barry Popik’s file records a September 1967 report in the Sunday Herald of Provo, Utah, in which Stephen R. Covey — then a university administrator, two decades before The Seven Habits — told students that “efficiency is doing things right and effectiveness is doing the right things.” No source is named in that report.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Peter Drucker can reasonably be credited with the efficiency-versus-effectiveness versions in his 1963 article, 1965 speech and 1974 book, and that Warren Bennis should receive credit for the versions contrasting leading and managing as in his 1997 book.

Quote Investigator transcribes the 1974 Harper & Row edition of Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices, Chapter 4 'The Dimensions of Management', page 45 (bibliographic note: 'Verified with scans'), reading: 'Effectiveness is the foundation of success—efficiency is a minimum condition for survival after success has been achieved. Efficiency is concerned with doing things right. Effectiveness is doing the right things.'

Quote Investigator records an 1869 Harrisburg Telegraph filler item ('There is a difference between doing a thing right, and doing the right thing') and a 1934 Elsie Robinson column ('You think efficiency means doing things right... IT MEANS KNOWING WHAT IS THE RIGHT THING TO DO'), noting the word 'effectiveness' was absent from both.

Quote Investigator quotes Drucker's May 1963 Harvard Business Review article 'Managing for Business Effectiveness': 'It is fundamentally the confusion between effectiveness and efficiency that stands between doing the right things and doing things right', and quotes a 1965 Financial Post digest of a Drucker lecture at the University of Toronto: 'Efficiency attempts to do things right... Effectiveness is concerned with doing the right things... A business can easily die of inefficiency. But no business can survive, let alone grow, because it is efficient.'

Quote Investigator quotes Stephen R. Covey's The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), page 101, attributing 'Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things' to both Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis, and quotes Bennis's 1997 Managing People Is Like Herding Cats using the leading/managing wording.

hbr.org hosts the article 'Managing for Business Effectiveness' by Peter F. Drucker, Harvard Business Review, May 1963; the efficiency/effectiveness sentence itself is not visible in the free preview.

Barry Popik's entry states that 'Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things' has been credited to Peter Drucker (1909-2005), 'who said something like this in 1960s lectures and in his book, The Effective Executive (1967)', credits 'Managers do things right; leaders do the right thing' to Warren G. Bennis and Burt Nanus in Leaders: The Strategies for Taking Charge (1985), and records a 10 September 1967 Sunday Herald (Provo, UT) report of Stephen R. Covey telling students that 'efficiency is doing things right and effectiveness is doing the right things'.
The Internet Archive holds a scanned, borrowable copy of Management: tasks, responsibilities, practices by Peter F. Drucker, Harper & Row, New York, 1974, 874 pages.

Wikipedia describes Peter Ferdinand Drucker (19 November 1909 – 11 November 2005) as an Austrian American management consultant, educator, and author, born in Vienna and died in Claremont, California, and lists Management: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices (New York: Harper & Row) in his bibliography dated 1973.
